title: LLawCo: Learning Laws of Cooperation for Modeling Embodied Multi-Agent Behavior
one_liner: Teach cooperating agents a short set of reusable behavior rules so they stay aligned with teammates and the shared task.
lead: In a shared task, each agent sees only part of the situation and must act while guessing what partners know and plan to do. That often breaks cooperation because one agent speaks too much, moves too early, or waits when the group needs action. This paper studies whether agents can learn compact behavior rules from past failures so that later decisions stay aligned with both teammates and the task goal.

problem.h2: Cooperation fails when each agent acts from a private partial view
paras: Embodied multi-agent tasks are hard because each agent sees only part of the room, part of the object state, or part of the dialogue. A locally sensible action can still hurt the team because a partner may be waiting for a signal, occupying the same path, or handling a different subtask.

Many language-based agents treat every new turn as a fresh writing problem. That makes coordination brittle because the agent may not carry forward simple team rules such as when to speak, when to wait, and when to hand work to a partner. The paper asks whether these recurring rules can be extracted from failures and then reused in later episodes.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Turn repeated coordination failures into short reusable cooperation rules, then train agents to consult those rules during later decision making because stable team habits reduce avoidable mismatch.

panels.title: 1. Two agents share a task
panels.viz_args: Each agent sees part of the scene and part of the conversation.
panels.caption: No single agent has the full state, so teamwork depends on timely alignment.

panels.title: 2. They drift apart
panels.viz_args: One moves early, one waits, and neither explains enough.
panels.caption: The task stalls because individually sensible actions can still clash at the team level.

panels.title: 3. Past failures are reviewed
panels.caption: The system looks for recurring mismatch patterns because repeated failure often points to a missing team rule.

panels.title: 4. A short rule is written
panels.viz_args: Examples: speak when needed, wait for partner, confirm before acting.
panels.caption: The rule is short enough to reuse because it summarizes a pattern instead of a whole episode.

panels.title: 5. Later episodes go smoother
panels.viz_args: The agents consult the learned rules while planning their next turns.
panels.caption: Cooperation improves because the team now carries forward lessons about timing and communication.

steps.text: Collect interaction traces from cooperative tasks where agents must talk and act under partial observability.
Look for repeated coordination mistakes so that training can focus on patterns that matter more than one-off accidents.
Turn those patterns into short statements such as when to wait or when to communicate because reusable rules are easier to carry across tasks than full transcripts.

steps.b: Insert the rules into decision making
steps.text: Expose the rules during supervised fine-tuning so that later action selection is nudged toward team-aligned reasoning.
Measure task success and cooperation efficiency so that the result shows whether the rules improve both outcome and teamwork quality.

paras: The paper changes what gets reused across episodes. Instead of reusing an entire past trajectory, it reuses distilled coordination laws that describe how teammates should behave under common situations.
object.object: the reusable unit of experience in multi-agent cooperation

hidden.name: how aligned each agent's next move is with the partner's likely needs
paras: The main hidden quantity is alignment between one agent's next move and the teammate's needs. You cannot read that quantity directly because the agents never output a numeric alignment score during normal play.

You infer it from behavior: whether an agent waits at the right time, sends a needed message, or avoids interfering with a partner. The paper tries to raise that hidden quantity by learning explicit cooperation rules from past breakdowns so that future decisions are constrained by team-level lessons.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark decisions where small timing differences strongly affect coordination quality.

reads.html: The hidden question is whether my next move helps my partner right now because it matches what they need, or surprises them because it breaks that expectation.
The method improves cooperative alignment by turning repeated mismatch cases into explicit rules, which means later choices are filtered through team-level guidance instead of only local impulse.

mechanism.h2: Why extracted cooperation laws can help
paras: Whole trajectories are often too specific to reuse because the room layout, object positions, and partner observations change from episode to episode. A short rule can transfer more widely because it captures the reason a failure happened rather than the exact surface details of one run.

Training on those rules can help because the agent gets repeated practice connecting local observations to team obligations. That matters in partial-information settings because the agent must often act on what the teammate probably needs, not only on what it personally sees.

stages.s: Rewrite them as compact cooperation laws
Train agents to consult those laws during planning

math.h2: A simple way to view the objective
math.words: Episode quality can be viewed as task completion minus coordination mistakes, because a team succeeds only when it both reaches the goal and avoids getting in its own way.
symbols: overall quality of one cooperative episode
how much of the shared goal the agents completed
penalty from acting out of sync with the partner or the task state

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a team completes most of the task, so task completion is 9.
Suppose it also makes two harmful coordination mistakes worth 3 total cost.
Then episode score is 9 minus 3, which gives 6.
If a learned rule removes one of those mistakes, mismatch cost might drop to 1.
Then the score rises to 8 because the same task progress is achieved with less interference.

math.note: The paper contains a richer training setup, but this equation captures the core idea that cooperation quality matters alongside raw task completion.

charts.title: Without learned cooperation laws
charts.note: The point of this baseline is to show how often teams drift when they lack stable shared rules.

charts.title: With learned cooperation laws
charts.note: The desired result is better team coordination because the rules remove recurring mismatch that used to waste turns.

items.b: The learned rules can be too generic.
items.html: A short rule may miss important context, so an agent can follow it in the wrong situation because the original failure pattern was oversimplified.

items.b: Failure review can inherit bad judgments.
items.html: If the system mislabels the reason an episode failed, it may write the wrong law and repeat that mistake later because training reinforces the wrong explanation.

items.b: Rules can conflict with each other.
items.html: One law may say to wait while another says to report immediately, so the agent needs a way to resolve tension because otherwise the law set becomes inconsistent.
The method is useful when cooperation failures repeat across tasks, because then a small number of clear laws can remove a large share of avoidable mismatch.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a two-agent room task where each side sees different objects and must coordinate to finish a shared objective. Log failures where the agents collide, wait too long, or omit needed messages. Then derive a short law set from those failures and retrain the agents with the laws present during decision making.

The demo should compare success rate, average extra turns, and count of coordination mistakes. It should show that the law-trained agents finish more tasks because they spend fewer turns undoing avoidable partner mismatch.
demo.metric_eq: coordination_gain = mismatch_cost_before - mismatch_cost_after ; success_gain = success_after - success_before
demo.closing: The point of the demo is to show that distilled cooperation rules help because they carry forward the reason earlier teamwork failed.
